newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia cautiously optimistic over G7 summit gains.
newsitem.headline: Russia cautiously optimistic over G7 summit gains.

text.p: Pro-government politicians on Monday hailed the Group of Seven summit in Denvier as a huge success for President Boris Yeltsin, but other political forces were far more cautious.

"The president got what he wanted and even more," Vladimir Ryzhkov, a senior member of the pro-government Our Home is Russia party, told reporters, referring to Yeltsin's participation in virtually the entire summit.
The Group of Seven leading industrialised nations -- Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States -- excluded Russia from just one session of financial talks.
Yeltsin, in common with virtually all officials and Russian media commentators, has said the gathering marks the start of a "Group of Eight".

The president, who arrived home on Monday, won a promise from Western leaders to admit Russia to the Paris Club of creditor states. They also pledged to help it join other major international economic and financial institutions, such as the World Trade Organisation.
"We see the Denver meeting as a tremendous success for Russia and hope that its integration in what is now the Group of Eight will go ahead smoothly," said Ryzhkov.
Other political parties at both ends of Russia's political spectrum declined to share Ryzhkov's optimism.
"All these summits are drowned out by fanfares," Communist Alexei Podberyozkin said. "The West welcomed (Soviet leader Leonid) Brezhnev with no less fuss than they now welcome Yeltsin."

"But in the real world the way they treat the national leader largely depends on what kind of country he leads," he added. "From that point of view, we can only hope to be accepted by the West as a junior partner, nothing more."
Sergei Ivanenko, deputy chairman of the Yabloko party, a fierce liberal opponent of both Yeltsin and the Communists, shared Podberyozkin's views.
"We could get much more if we had a stronger economy, a more consolidated society, a wiser parliament and a more effective government," Ivanenko said.
But he said his party still saw Russia's stronger involvement in the G7 as a positive step.

Pro-government politicians and liberal media agreed the warm welcome Yeltsin received in Denver could help his reformist cabinet -- spearheaded by youthful first deputy prime ministers Anatoly Chubais and Boris Nemtsov -- to push forward economic reforms.

"Germany lost World War Two but was helped by the Marshall Plan," Ryzhkov said, referring to U.S. aid to post-war Europe. "That country put aside its pride and used the help to rise from ashes. We now have to be pragmatic and follow suit."

The government has announced bold plans to sweep away remnants of the centralised, paternalistic Soviet system that still impede the transition to a full-scale market economy. Yeltsin's team is now trying to push crucial reform legislation through the Communist-dominated parliament.
The newspaper Komsomolskaya Pravda said the success of economic reforms, among other things, would have a decisive impact on Russia's future role in the G7.

"Only when the projects of the respected Mr Chubais start to bear fruit, long cherished by all Russians, will they have any hope of realising the dream of equal partnership with 'dear friends' Bill and Helmut," it wrote, referring to U.S. President Clinton and German Chancellor Kohl.
